meta.notes: Layer 2 experiments on the network scenarios. Station utilisation comes straight from the engine; labour-pool utilisation is derived by grouping the stations that share a skill and dividing their busy minutes by the pre-break shift minutes of the staff that can operate them. Cells with an estimated peak load above 0.95 use 60 replicates (the saturated tea capacities), everything else uses 100; first seed 0, stride 1. The balk decision uses the engine's Little's-Law-style wait estimate divided by the number of staff units that are ON SHIFT at the arrival instant (shift windows and breaks are coverage-checked), so a late-joining barista does not make the shop look bigger than it is; the legacy v1 path keeps the full worker count so the golden anchors stay bit-identical.

bottleneck_migration.note: With staff synced to stations the tea station stays the busiest station for every capacity, but each extra station pays for itself only up to the computed critical capacity; beyond it the shared barista pool and the order counter take over the queue. The fixed-labour companion is the clean picture of the migration: with the barista count held fixed, tea station utilisation collapses as slots are added while mean waiting, p95 and profit are bit-identical, because the labour pool is now the constraint.

strategy_by_bottleneck.note: Fast-item priority is worth much less when the tea station is the bottleneck than when the ice-cream machine is: the fast lane only helps customers whose own station has slack.

skill_matrix.note: Same headcount and the same wage bill in all three cells, so the difference is pure queueing: a single flexible pool captures the pooling gain, one-way cross-training into the under-loaded task does not.

shifts.note: Breaks near a peak cost more than they save: a staggered 30-minute break removes capacity exactly when the peak needs it, so the peak-hour wait and the p95 jump and profit falls by more than the unpaid break saves in wages. Adding a barista mid-shift raises served and lowers balking, but the afternoon peak wait is essentially unchanged because the tea station, not headcount, is the binding resource at the peak; the extra wage line therefore costs money. Before minute 240 the mid-shift variant is identical to the no-shift baseline (the extra barista is not on shift and the balk estimate only counts staff on shift), so the morning peak is unchanged by construction rather than by luck.
